chunks: Abu Ali Al-Ash'ari, from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Jabbar, from Safwan, who said:

Al-Husayn ibn Mahran asked Abu Al-Hasan Al-Rida (peace be upon him) about a man who performed Zahir from four women, so he (peace be upon him) said: 'He must expiate for each one of them with an expiation.'

And he asked him (peace be upon him) about a man who performed Zahir from his wife and his slave girl, 'What is upon him?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'Upon him for each one of them is an expiation: freeing a neck, or fasting two consecutive months, or feeding sixty poor people.'

key_terms.إِطْعَامُ سِتِّينَ مِسْكِيناً: It'am Sittin Miskinan: Feeding sixty poor people.
key_terms.صِيَامُ شَهْرَيْنِ مُتَتَابِعَيْنِ: Siyam Shahrayn Mutatabaynayn: Fasting for two consecutive months.
key_terms.ظَاهَرَ: Zahir: A form of divorce in Islamic law where a man likens his wife's back to his mother's back, prohibiting sexual relations until expiation is made.
key_terms.كَفَّارَةً: Kaffarah: Expiation or atonement required for specific acts or oaths.

ai.seo_question: What is the expiation for Zahir when a man performs it with multiple wives or slaves?
ai.summary: This hadith clarifies the jurisprudential principle that the expiation (Kaffarah) for Zahir is per individual rather than per act, requiring separate expiations for each of the four wives or the wife and concubine. It highlights the Shia scholarly consensus on the equivalence of the three expiation options—freeing a slave, fasting two consecutive months, or feeding sixty poor people—while noting the historical context of concubinage (Jariyah) in early Islamic society. The ruling underscores the seriousness of the Zahir vow as a form of irrevocable separation, distinct from standard divorce, necessitating specific atonement to restore marital or relational permissibility.
